extracted.intended_audience: Citizens and voters of New York; readers evaluating the proposed U.S. Constitution (general public interested in constitutional design)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and practical principles for structuring the national Executive, the Senate’s role in impeachments, and the mode of electing the President under the proposed Constitution. Focuses on separation of powers, checks and balances, electoral mechanisms, and limits on executive authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial intermixture of departments
rubrics_metrics.description: The departments of government may have a partial intermixture for special purposes while remaining distinct and unconnected in the main.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such partial intermixture is sometimes proper or necessary to the mutual defense of the several members of government against each other; it preserves distinctness while enabling checks and balances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive negative (qualified veto) as indispensable barrier
rubrics_metrics.description: An absolute or qualified negative in the executive upon acts of the legislative body is an indispensable barrier against legislative encroachments upon the executive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The veto (qualified negative) operates as an essential counterpoise to legislative power and helps maintain separation of functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of impeachment powers (House accuses, Senate judges)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign the right of instituting impeachments to one legislative branch and the right of judging them to the other to avoid making the same persons both accusers and judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This division guards against persecution from factious spirit and the danger of combining accusation and judgment in the same body; requiring two-thirds of the Senate for conviction secures additional protection for innocence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate as proper tribunal for impeachments
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate, together with certain judiciary officers in some states, has historical precedent as a court of impeachments and is a fit receptacle for trying impeachments at the national level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument from practice in state constitutions (e.g., New York) and from the avoidance of mixing accuser and judge; the Senate’s composition and modes of appointment support its fitness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterbalances to Senate power: House privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide specific counterpoises to any additional authorities conferred upon the Senate (e.g., exclusive privilege of originating money bills assigned to the House).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The House’s exclusive initiation of money bills and sole right to institute impeachments act as complete counterbalances to Senate authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: House’s contingent powers as influence (electing President)
rubrics_metrics.description: The House’s authority to decide the President when no candidate secures a majority of electors is an important source of influence and counterweight to the Senate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The possibility that the House may choose the President from the top five electoral vote recipients gives the House ongoing significance and influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popularity as a natural counterpoise
rubrics_metrics.description: The most popular branch of government (the House) will generally be a full match or overmatch for other members of government, providing an operative check on senatorial influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples and the nature of popularity are invoked to show that popular branches restrain others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate’s advice-and-consent is not a choosing power
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate’s role in appointments is to advise and consent—ratify or reject the President’s nominations—not to choose officers itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the Senate cannot make the initial choice (only the President nominates), the Senate’s agency lacks the same favoritism one would expect if it selected appointees itself; it may defeat a nomination but cannot substitute its own candidate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recess-appointment clause applies to officers, not Senators
rubrics_metrics.description: The clause permitting the President to fill vacancies during the recess refers to 'officers of the United States' whose appointments are not otherwise provided for, and thus does not extend to senators whose appointment is otherwise provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The clause is supplementary to the general appointment clause; state executives are expressly given power to fill Senate vacancies temporarily, which excludes the President from filling Senate seats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint agency in treaties as check by character and numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Security against corruption in treaty formation is sought in the joint agency of the Chief Magistrate and two-thirds of the Senate — the number and character of the persons who make treaties are the pledge of fidelity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impeachment of a large collective (e.g., two-thirds of a legislature) is impracticable; collective responsibility is secured by confiding trust to proper hands and making combination against public good difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral principle: people’s sense should operate
rubrics_metrics.description: It is desirable that the sense of the people should operate in choosing the Chief Magistrate; the right should be committed to men chosen by the people for the special purpose (electors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures that the popular will is represented indirectly while preventing direct tumult and enabling selection by persons capable of deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electors should be capable and deliberative
rubrics_metrics.description: Electors should be persons chosen by the people who are most capable of analyzing the qualities adapted to the Presidency and acting under circumstances favorable to deliberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A small, select body of electors will better analyze qualities and weigh competing reasons than a direct mass election for such a complex trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral design to avoid tumult, disorder, corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing several electors to form an intermediate body, assembled within their states, reduces the risk of tumult, disorder, and corruption and of foreign tampering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dispersed electors are less prone to sudden combinations or corrupt influence; exclusion of senators, representatives, and federal officeholders from being electors limits bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of the Executive via re-election mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: The Executive should be independent for continuance in office on all but the people themselves; re-election should depend on a special body deputed by society to the single purpose of making the choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents the President from sacrificing duty for complaisance to those whose favor is necessary for continuance; the electoral mechanism helps secure independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contingent House selection to ensure qualified President
rubrics_metrics.description: If no candidate secures a majority of electors, the House selecting from the five highest vote-getters provides a mechanism to ensure an appropriately qualified President.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contingency complements the electoral mechanism to avoid having the office fall to someone without majority support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral selection tends to promote eminent qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: The process produces a moral certainty that the Presidency will be filled by persons eminent in ability and virtue rather than by talent for low intrigue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being chosen by a national body of electors requires broader esteem and different merits than state-level popularity; it elevates candidates of national reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vice-President chosen similarly with distinct rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: The Vice-President is to be chosen in the same manner as the President, rather than by election from the Senate, to preserve the casting vote of the Senate and to ensure the Vice-President is eligible as a substitute for the President.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting the Vice-President by electors prevents turning a senator into a constant instead of contingent vote for his state and applies the same merits-requirements as for the President.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive structure: single magistrate with term limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Vest executive authority in a single magistrate elected for four years and re-eligible; differs from hereditary monarchy and resembles state governors in elective character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A limited, renewable term reduces the danger of dangerous influence compared to hereditary monarchy; comparison with state governors shows continuity of republican principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive accountability and impeachment
rubrics_metrics.description: The President should be liable to impeachment, trial, removal for high crimes and misdemeanors, and afterwards to prosecution in ordinary law — personal responsibility unlike monarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures the Chief Magistrate is not above the law; contrasts with the inviolability of a king who has no constitutional tribunal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualified veto vs. absolute prerogative
rubrics_metrics.description: The President’s power to return a bill for reconsideration (qualified negative) differs greatly from the British sovereign’s absolute negative and is a more limited check.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A qualified veto allows legislative override (two-thirds) and is analogous to revisionary powers elsewhere (e.g., state councils), not an absolute monarchical prerogative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commander-in-chief powers are limited
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is commander-in-chief of the army and navy and of the militia when called into actual service of the Union, but lacks unilateral power to declare war or to raise and regulate fleets and armies (legislative domain).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The President’s military authority is supreme in command but subordinate to legislative powers of declaring war and regulating forces; militia authority is conditional on call into service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pardoning power limited by impeachment exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The President has power to grant reprieves and pardons for offenses against the United States except in cases of impeachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This restriction ensures that impeachment remains a separate constitutional remedy for official misconduct and cannot be nullified by the pardon power.
